title: King v. Villegas en banc: a no contest plea to resisting does not end a prisoner's force suit, plus a bystander's camera in Texas and pepper spray on a self-harming inmate
summary: The Ninth Circuit's full court decided King v. Villegas on November 24: a Kern Valley State Prison inmate who pleaded no contest to resisting an officer may still sue the two correctional officers for excessive force, because a no contest plea admits no facts and success on the force claim would not necessarily imply the conviction was invalid. The court overruled part of Sanders v. City of Pittsburg. Six judges joined the opinion, three concurred in the judgment only and warned the holding could keep Heck v. Humphrey from applying in no contest cases, and two dissented, one of them closing with "So long, Heck." Elsewhere, the Fifth Circuit held in Berg v. Rivas that a San Antonio officer's six second spotlight on a bystander's phone camera and a second officer's perimeter around a traffic stop were not enough to support a First Amendment retaliation claim, while confirming that recording the police is protected activity. The Seventh Circuit held in McNamara v. King that pepper spraying a Wisconsin prisoner who was standing on his sink and harming himself was a good faith effort to restore order, not excessive force. The Supreme Court issued no force decision or order this holiday week, and no California published decision addressed force.
coverage: Checked: the Ninth Circuit's own list of published opinions for November 23 through 27, read from the court's website on Saturday, November 28. King v. Villegas was read in full from the court's PDF, all 62 pages including the concurrence and both dissents. The week's two other custody decisions, Ewalan v. Washington Department of Corrections (November 24, appointment of counsel in a failure to protect case, with a dissent by Judge Bumatay) and Murillo v. Castillo (November 25, grievance exhaustion and joinder at Salinas Valley State Prison), were opened and are not force holdings. The remaining published opinions (USA v. Tran, USA v. Ramirez, Yount v. Whole Foods Market, Rolovich v. Washington State University, Sunday Red v. Tigeraire, Los Molinos Mutual Water Company v. Ekdahl, Estate of Daher v. LSH Co., Honolulu Civil Beat v. The court's memoranda list shows only the most recent 25 dispositions, and this week they reached back to November 23, so the whole week was visible.

sections.heading: Ninth Circuit
sections.note: One decision, and it is the biggest custody force ruling from this court in some time: the full eleven judge court sat on King v. Villegas and split three ways over whether a prisoner's no contest plea to resisting an officer bars his excessive force suit under Heck v. Humphrey. The court's two other custody decisions this week are procedural. Ewalan v. Washington Department of Corrections vacated a defense verdict in a failure to protect case because the district court should have appointed substitute counsel for a prisoner with a traumatic brain injury, over a dissent by Judge Bumatay, and Murillo v. Castillo is about grievance exhaustion and joinder at Salinas Valley State Prison. Neither decides anything about force, and neither is covered further.

cases.name: King v. Villegas
cases.court: Ninth Circuit, en banc (from the Eastern District of California, Judge Jennifer L. Thurston)
cases.topic: Heck v. Humphrey and prison excessive force; a no contest plea to resisting an executive officer under Penal Code section 69; Sanders v. City of Pittsburg overruled in part
cases.caution: Read in full from the court's PDF, including Judge Owens' concurrence and the dissents of Judge Collins and Judge VanDyke. The case was decided on the pleadings, so the court took the prisoner's allegations as true and said so; nothing in the opinion finds that the officers did what he alleges. The opinion presents the officers' version from their incident reports alongside the prisoner's, and both are given below. The court decided only whether the suit may proceed. It did not decide whether any force was excessive.
cases.facts: On August 17, 2016, Jerry Lee King, newly transferred to Kern Valley State Prison and on orientation status, was being escorted with about nine other new arrivals to another building by Officer R. Villegas and a second officer. The two accounts diverge from there. King's pro se complaint says the inmates were handcuffed, that an inmate behind him asked a question and he answered, and that Villegas approached and said, "What don't you understand about shut your fucking mouth?" King replied that Villegas did not have to get in his face and talk to him that way. Then, "without any provocation," Villegas grabbed King by the back of his shirt and "with great force" "rammed [King]'s head into the wall" with his forearm, splitting his head open. King said "what the fuck," and Villegas swept his feet, took him to the ground, and yelled a code one assault on staff. Officer P. Cruz responded and, "while [King] was l[y]ing on the ground," "struck [him] with great force and a close[d] fist in his right eye" and ground his ankles into the asphalt. King alleged a sergeant later told medical staff to document that he had "refused treatment." He was placed in solitary confinement. The officers' incident reports say King was not handcuffed, was facing the wall and talking loudly while other inmates checked in, was told to be quiet, and then "without warning or provocation" swung both arms upward, twisted, and struck Villegas's right shoulder with his right hand, continuing to twist and try to elbow him. Villegas pushed King toward the wall to secure him in handcuffs, which caused King's head to strike the wall. Cruz forced King to the ground in a prone position, Villegas landed on top of him, King kept struggling, Villegas announced a Code 1 staff battery by radio, Cruz held his legs, and King then stopped and complied with orders to put his hands behind his back. All three were medically examined and another officer took photographs; the court noted that "[n]o photographs are in the record on appeal." A prison disciplinary hearing found King guilty of battery on a peace officer. King filed his section 1983 suit in May 2017. Several months later, and more than a year after the incident, Kern County charged him with battery by a prisoner on a non-confined person and with resisting an executive officer under Penal Code section 69; the federal case was stayed. The criminal case took nearly five years. In March 2022 King entered a no contest plea under People v. West to the section 69 count for an eight month sentence, and the battery count was dismissed. At the plea hearing the judge described the plea as "I don't really admit" and "kind of like no contest on steroids," King said "I don't want [my plea] to affect my civil case in any way," his lawyer said the West plea "is intended so that it won't impact the civil suit" but could not promise that, and counsel stipulated to a factual basis "based on the probable cause statement and the reports in discovery with the understanding this is a People vs. West and a no contest plea." The officers then moved for judgment on the pleadings under Heck. A magistrate judge and the first district judge denied the motion; after reassignment, Judge Thurston granted it, finding "there is no possible way these two sets of facts could simultaneously be true." A three judge panel reversed on Federal Rule of Evidence 410 grounds, and the court took the case en banc.
cases.holding: Reversed and remanded, in an opinion by Judge W. Fletcher. Heck bars a civil claim only where a favorable judgment would "necessarily imply the invalidity of [a] conviction or sentence," and the court began from common ground: "success on a civil excessive force claim against an officer under § 1983 is not necessarily inconsistent with a valid conviction for resisting that officer," because "the officer used too much force to respond to the assault [or resistance] or that the officer used force after the need for force had disappeared." Under California law a section 69 or section 148 conviction requires that the officer was acting lawfully, so a force claim is barred "if the force that the plaintiff challenges as unlawful is the same force that the plaintiff was convicted of resisting." The court's earlier en banc cases, Lemos and Smith v. City of Hemet, involved a jury verdict and a guilty plea, where facts were proven or admitted, and the court looked at the record to see which acts formed the basis of the conviction. A no contest plea is different. It "is a special creature under the law" and is "first and foremost, not an admission of factual guilt." The question, the court said, "is whether, in a civil suit under § 1983, a plaintiff who pleaded nolo to a state criminal charge will be bound to a factual narrative that was never proven and whose truth he never admitted. As we explain below, the answer is no." Because King's "guilt was neither proven nor admitted," "[t]here is therefore no factual narrative to which King is bound," and "[t]o the extent that the three-judge panel opinion in Sanders v. City of Pittsburg, 14 F.4th 968 (9th Cir. 2021), can be read as holding otherwise, it is overruled." The conviction still presupposes a prima facie factual basis for the charge, so the claim would be barred if success were "logically incompatible with the existence of a prima facie basis for the criminal charge against him." It was not. The district court had described King as alleging he was "not resisting the entire time," but "King did not write the words quoted in the brief"; he alleged he was not resisting at one point, when Cruz struck him in the eye, and wrote that he never provoked the officers. "Never resisting (as Defendants-Appellees would have it) and never provoking (as King wrote) are distinct." A factfinder could find excessive force at another point, "for example, when Villegas allegedly 'rammed [King]'s head into the wall,' or when Cruz was allegedly 'grinding the Plaintiff's ankles' into the ground," because resistance "may precede or follow the excessive use of force by that same officer even within 'a single continuous chain of events lasting a very brief time.'" The court added a limit: "We do not hold that the Heck bar will never apply when a conviction is based on a nolo plea under CPC § 1192.5." It did not reach Rule 410. Judge Owens, joined by Judges Miller and Forrest, concurred in the judgment only. He would have let King amend his complaint to say which acts of force and which officer he is suing over, then had the district court run the Lemos analysis, and he warned that "if left unchecked, the majority's holding could effectively prevent Heck from applying in nolo cases. This is a dramatic change in how judges have applied this doctrine for decades and will have significant ramifications in our federal and state trial courts."
cases.dissent: Judge Collins, joined by Judge VanDyke and joined as to his first two parts by Judges Owens, Miller, and Forrest, would have affirmed. In his view the majority's account of California no contest pleas is "profoundly wrong": Penal Code section 1016(3) makes the legal effect of a no contest plea to a felony punishable offense "the same as that of a plea of guilty for all purposes," the California Supreme Court has called the contrary argument "specious," and a People v. West plea "simply means that the plea was the result of a plea bargain." The factual basis here was counsel's stipulation to the probable cause statement and the reports, which "cover all of the resistive conduct described by the officers over the course of the entire incident," so all of the officers' conduct during that resistance was lawful for Heck purposes and every one of King's allegations is inconsistent with it. To call the difference between never provoking and never resisting "a technical difference," he wrote, "is to read the complaint casuistically rather than reasonably." Judge VanDyke, dissenting separately, called the case "a tale of two stories" and said the court has developed a "slice-and-dice" approach that lets a judge "transform one continuous officer-defendant incident into a theoretically limitless number of sub-incidents." King's complaint, he wrote, "tells a tale of unlawful conduct from start to finish," so the majority had to rest on a hypothetical that King resisted at some other point, a possibility that "exists only if you turn on 'track changes' and redline King's complaint for him." He cited the Fifth, Seventh, and Tenth Circuits and the California Supreme Court for the rule that a plaintiff who pleads a wholly unprovoked attack pleads into the Heck bar, and he closed: "So long, Heck. It's been nice knowing you."
cases.notDecided: Whether any force was excessive. The case was decided on the pleadings, the officers' reports tell a different story, and the court took King's allegations as true because it had to. Whether Rule 410 bars a court from considering a no contest plea and the plea hearing for Heck purposes; the panel had said yes, and the en banc court did not reach it. Whether Heck can ever bar a claim after a no contest plea; the court said it was not holding that the bar never applies, only that it does not apply here. What California law makes of a West plea in a state court civil suit; the court said that is a state law question it was not deciding. Whether King's prison disciplinary finding has any effect on the suit.
cases.inPractice: For custody staff, the headline is simple: in the Ninth Circuit, a prisoner's no contest plea to resisting staff no longer closes the civil case over the same incident. Officers and agencies that have treated a criminal disposition as the end of the civil exposure should stop doing so for no contest pleas, and the same reasoning reaches a street arrest that ends in a no contest plea to section 69 or section 148. What follows from that is about reports. King's officers wrote reports that became the factual basis for the plea, and those reports will now be tested against his complaint in front of a factfinder. The majority's analysis works moment by moment: resistance at one point, force at another, and the question is whether the force at each point was lawful. The dissents call that slicing and dicing, but it is the law of the circuit, and the report that survives it is the one that describes the sequence in order with the resistance that preceded each application of force and the point at which the resistance stopped. The officers' reports here did that in outline: strikes to the shoulder, an attempt to elbow, a push to the wall, a takedown to prone, continued struggling, a radio call, legs controlled, hands behind the back, cuffs, relief by other staff. The second practical point is the record that was not there. The court noted that photographs were taken and that none were in the record on appeal, and King alleged a sergeant told medical staff to document a refusal of treatment. Injury photographs of the inmate and of staff, the medical evaluations, and any refusal documented in the inmate's own words are the evidence that answers an allegation like that one. Third, the plea hearing itself is instructive. King asked twice whether the plea would affect his civil case, the judge said he did not know, and defense counsel said the West plea was intended not to affect it. Prosecutors and agency liaisons should understand that a stipulation to the reports as the factual basis for a no contest plea does not bind the plaintiff to those reports in federal court. Finally, read the vote. Six judges joined the opinion, three joined only the judgment and said the holding "could effectively prevent Heck from applying in nolo cases," and five judges joined the parts of the Collins dissent that call the majority's reading of California plea law wrong. Expect the losing side to seek further review, and expect district courts to follow the majority in the meantime.
cases.trainIt: Teach the rule in one sentence: a resisting conviction and an excessive force claim can both be true, and a no contest plea admits no facts at all. Pair King with Smith v. City of Hemet from the Case library, where the full court said the same thing about a guilty plea under section 148, so staff hear that this is not new; what is new is that a no contest plea no longer carries a factual narrative into the civil case. Then train the report. Walk through the officers' account in King as a sequence and have staff mark every point where force was applied and name the resistance that preceded it; then mark the point where the inmate complied and the force changed to control and handcuffing. That is the report that survives a moment by moment review. Train the evidence package after a staff assault: photographs of the inmate and of staff, the medical evaluations, and any refusal of treatment recorded in the inmate's own words, with the inmate's signature where policy allows. Teach supervisors how King's complaint used the medical record: an allegation that a sergeant told medical staff what to write is answered by a record that shows who wrote it and when. For patrol trainers, run the same lesson with a section 148 arrest: the no contest plea the prosecutor offers to clear the case does not end the civil suit, and the report is still the officer's best evidence. Teach the posture accurately: the case was decided on the pleadings, nothing has been found about the force, and the court said Heck can still bar some claims after a no contest plea.

sections.heading: Other federal circuits
sections.note: Two unpublished decisions, neither binding precedent, each useful in a briefing. Berg is a bystander recording case from a San Antonio traffic stop that turns on the difference between a six second spotlight and a continuous obstruction of the camera. McNamara is a Wisconsin prison case about pepper spray used on a prisoner who was standing on his sink and harming himself, decided at the screening stage under the Hudson v. McMillian good faith standard.

cases.name: Berg v. Rivas
cases.court: Fifth Circuit (from the Western District of Texas)
cases.topic: A bystander recording a traffic stop; First Amendment retaliation; a spotlight aimed at the camera and a perimeter around the stop; qualified immunity and Monell
cases.caution: Read in full from the court's PDF. The decision is not designated for publication and is not binding precedent. The case was decided on the complaint, with the bystander's own cell phone video considered as part of the record because his complaint relied on it. This is a First Amendment case, not a force case; it is covered because the conduct at issue, managing a person recording an active stop, is a daily patrol task.
cases.facts: On April 11, 2024, at about 10:36 p.m., Kevin Berg and his wife stopped at a San Antonio gas station where a traffic stop was underway. When Berg came out of the store the stop "appeared to have escalated beyond a routine traffic stop," and he began recording on his phone from beside his parked car at a pump, in a well lit area. Officer Thomas Rivas stepped away from the stop and confronted him: "Hey, bro. Can you get outta here? Huh? Can you get outta here? Can you get outta here, or no?" When Berg asked why Rivas was talking to him, Rivas said, "Why are you recording? Why are you recording? You must have no f*ckin' life, right? Get out of here, dude." Rivas assigned another officer to stand by Berg and watch him. Several minutes later Rivas turned his vehicle spotlight onto Berg's camera for about six seconds; Berg moved "[a]lmost immediately" and kept recording from another spot. As he moved, Officer Manuel Gandara told him, "if you get near this traffic stop, you're gonna go to jail," and repeated twice that he would go to jail if he got closer. Berg stood in place and filmed for nearly the rest of the recording. He complained to the department two days later; a sergeant told him the only issue identified was Rivas's profanity, and after a demand letter a captain told him Rivas had been "reprimanded for language." Berg sued pro se under section 1983 for First Amendment retaliation against both officers and for Monell liability against the city. His complaint also alleged that other people, two men on foot, a red car at an adjacent pump, and a man who walked between the detained truck and the patrol car, came as close or closer without being told to leave. The district court dismissed everything and denied his motion to alter the judgment.
cases.holding: Affirmed, per curiam, by Judges Ho, Engelhardt, and Wilson. The first element of a retaliation claim was met: the district court "correctly determined that Berg's recording was constitutionally protected activity" under the circuit's Turner v. Lieutenant Driver decision. The case ended on the second element, whether the officers' actions "caused [Berg] to suffer an injury that would chill a person of ordinary firmness from continuing to engage in that activity." The court explained that the effect on speech "need not be great" to be actionable, but "some retaliatory actions—even if they actually have the effect of chilling the plaintiff's speech—are too trivial or minor to be actionable." The spotlight "curtailed Berg's speech, but 'trivial[ly]' so," and the perimeter "did not curtail Berg's speech at all." On the spotlight, the court compared its own unpublished decision in Rincon v. City of Laredo, where a six second confiscation of a phone was not enough, and distinguished Perkins v. Hart, where a deputy "moved from side to side to block" a recording, and the Tenth Circuit's Irizarry v. Yehia, where a flashlight "saturated the camera sensors" and made recording all but impossible. Rivas "did not move the spotlight from side to side to create a continuous obstruction"; "he turned it on, and Berg promptly moved aside. That distinction makes a difference." On the perimeter: it "simply delineated the area where he could continue to do so," and holding otherwise "would contort the right to film police, as expressed in Turner, into an entitlement to film officers from whatever angle and distance a plaintiff pleases. But the right to film the police 'is not without limitations.' Like all speech, filming the police 'may be subject to reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions.'" Berg's "completely uninterrupted recording following the alleged adverse conduct at least suggests that Rivas's conduct would not have chilled the speech of a person of ordinary firmness." With no constitutional violation, the officers had qualified immunity and the Monell claim against the city failed. The allegations that other bystanders were allowed closer could go only to retaliatory motive, which the court did not reach.
cases.notDecided: Whether the officers acted with retaliatory motive; the court stopped at the injury element. Whether Rivas's profanity, his order to leave, and his assignment of an officer to watch Berg would have been enough in combination; the court said the complaint pleaded only the order to leave and the spotlight as Rivas's adverse actions, and that Berg offered no case making the rest sufficient. Whether the body camera footage could be considered at the pleading stage; the court said it did not matter. Anything about the underlying traffic stop or any use of force.
cases.inPractice: Three things officers can take from Berg, in order of importance. First, the recording was protected. The Fifth Circuit said so in the first paragraph of its analysis, and the Ninth Circuit recognizes the same right to record officers in public places. A bystander with a phone at a gas pump, in a well lit area, outside the stop, is exercising a right, and the question is only how officers manage the scene around that right. Second, the line the court drew is between a momentary interference and an obstruction. Six seconds of spotlight that the man stepped out of was trivial; a flashlight that blinds the camera, or an officer who moves side to side to block it, has been enough in other courts. The practical rule is simple: do not point lights at cameras and do not block them. Third, a perimeter is a time, place, and manner restriction, and it held up here because it applied to the recording itself only in the sense that the man could not come closer. What the court did not reach is the allegation that other people were allowed closer without being told to leave. That allegation goes to motive, and in a case that clears the injury element it is the allegation that would decide the case. A perimeter that is enforced against the person with the camera and not against anyone else is the fact pattern to avoid. Finally, the words. "You must have no f*ckin' life, right?" earned a reprimand and a place in a federal opinion. The department's internal review found that the profanity was the only problem, and the court's result agrees, but the recording is the reason everyone knows what was said.
cases.trainIt: Train scene management with a recording bystander as a standard element of traffic stop scenarios: the trainee sets a perimeter, states it once in plain terms, applies it to everyone, and keeps lights and bodies off the camera. Debrief the two officers in Berg separately. Rivas's approach, the profanity, the order to leave, and the spotlight are the conduct that produced a complaint and a lawsuit; Gandara's perimeter warning, stated three times without profanity, is the conduct the court called a reasonable restriction. Teach the difference the court drew between a six second spotlight and a continuous obstruction, and teach that other courts have found a blinding flashlight or a body used to block a camera sufficient to state a claim. For supervisors, use the complaint handling as a second lesson: a sergeant's finding that profanity was the only issue, and a captain's letter that the officer had been reprimanded for language, were the department's record in the federal case. Teach the posture: unpublished, decided on the complaint, and silent on motive.

cases.name: McNamara v. King
cases.court: Seventh Circuit (from the Eastern District of Wisconsin)
cases.topic: Pepper spray on a prisoner standing on his sink and harming himself; Eighth Amendment excessive force under Hudson v. McMillian; screening dismissal
cases.caution: Read in full from the court's PDF. The decision is a nonprecedential order. The complaint was dismissed at screening, before the officers were served, so the court had only the prisoner's own account and took it as true. The officers did not participate in the appeal.
cases.facts: In August 2025, Sean McNamara, a prisoner at Green Bay Correctional Institution, began harming himself after learning that staff had searched his cell while he was away. He told an officer he had self-harmed, showed the blood on his arm, and asked for medical attention; the officer called for help. While waiting outside his cell he tapped small metal fragments from his window frame and swallowed them, along with a rubber pencil. Officer Marcus King arrived within minutes and took him to the health services unit, where staff treated his arm. McNamara asked to be sent offsite to have the metal removed; King refused, and McNamara described him as "very angry." McNamara was placed on observation status in restricted housing. A couple of hours later a doctor saw him by telehealth; he asked for a blanket because he was cold, and the doctor said she would consult King. Two hours after that King passed his cell, McNamara asked about the blanket, and King said, "yes maybe no, we will see how you act tonight." McNamara, who thought King was "messing with him," replied, "you must want me to freak out and hurt myself," climbed onto his sink, about three feet high, and began to harm himself again. King yelled at him, drew a taser and pointed it, and sent Officer David Johnson for pepper spray, instructing him to spray McNamara "if McNamara looked like he was going to jump off the sink or otherwise start to self-harm." McNamara began to harm himself while standing on the sink, and Johnson sprayed him in the eyes and the right side of his body. He could not see and fell off the sink, climbed back up, considered jumping so he could hit his head on the bed, decided not to, started to climb down, slipped, and fell again. Minutes later he was handcuffed and escorted down the hall, and another officer remarked, "wow that's a lot of spray." He sued King and Johnson under the Eighth Amendment and Wisconsin tort law. The district court dismissed the complaint at screening for failure to state a claim, declined supplemental jurisdiction over the state claims, and denied leave to amend as futile, including a later motion to add two unnamed officers for failure to intervene.
cases.holding: Affirmed, in a nonprecedential order by Judges Sykes, Jackson-Akiwumi, and Taibleson. The court applied the Hudson standard: "[w]henever prison officials stand accused of using excessive physical force in violation of the Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause, the core judicial inquiry is . . . whether force was applied in a good-faith effort to maintain or restore discipline, or maliciously and sadistically to cause harm." McNamara's "thorough characterization of the events does not allow a reasonable inference that the officers applied force for any reason other than to restore order to a situation that had grown alarming." The court pointed to his own allegations: "that he climbed up on the sink and began to harm himself, that King directed Johnson to use the pepper spray only if McNamara looked like he was about to jump or harm himself, and that only after he harmed himself did Johnson use the spray." Because his self-harm posed a risk to his safety, "the officers' use of pepper spray was not an 'unnecessary . . . infliction of pain' but a good-faith intervention to deescalate the situation and restore order." The court also upheld the denial of leave to amend, because McNamara did not say what new allegations would support a claim.
cases.notDecided: Whether the officers' account would match the prisoner's; they were never served and did not appear. Whether the amount of spray was excessive; the remark "wow that's a lot of spray" is in the complaint, and the court did not treat it as changing the analysis. Whether a failure to intervene claim against the unnamed officers would have survived; the court held only that the motion to add them came after judgment and did not explain how it would change the result. Any medical deliberate indifference claim about the swallowed metal, the refused offsite transport, or the blanket. The state law claims, which were dismissed without prejudice.
cases.inPractice: McNamara is a custody and juvenile hall case about the hardest kind of force decision: force used to stop a person from hurting himself. The court approved it under Hudson because the prisoner's own account showed three things. The instruction to use the spray was conditional, tied to a specific behavior, jumping or renewed self-harm. The spray was used only when that behavior resumed. And the force stopped there; he was handcuffed and escorted minutes later. Those are the facts that made the force a "good-faith intervention," and they are the facts a report in a self-harm response should contain. Two cautions. First, the exchange that preceded the escalation is also in the opinion. A blanket request routed through the doctor to the officer, an answer of "yes maybe no, we will see how you act tonight," and a prisoner who heard it as retaliation for an argument hours earlier is the sequence that put him on the sink. The court did not fault the officer for it, but a different plaintiff with a different record could plead the same words as evidence of malice. Second, the remark "wow that's a lot of spray" did not change this case at the screening stage, where the question was the officers' motive. In a case with a medical record, quantity and decontamination are facts a court will weigh, and the opinion says nothing about either. For juvenile detention, the same Hudson style good faith inquiry informs how courts look at force on a youth in crisis, and the lesson is identical: condition the force on the behavior, use it when the behavior happens, stop when it stops, and get medical staff to the youth.
cases.trainIt: Run a self-harm response scenario from this opinion: a prisoner on a fixture three feet off the floor, actively harming himself, who has already swallowed metal earlier in the shift. Train the supervising officer to state the condition out loud before any force, the way King did, so that every officer present and the record know what will trigger the spray and what will not. Train the report to capture the condition, the behavior that met it, the application, and the stop. Then debrief the blanket exchange. Ask officers how "we will see how you act tonight" sounds to a person who has already harmed himself twice that day and has swallowed metal fragments, and offer the alternative: answer the medical question as a medical question and route it back to the doctor. Teach the medical side of the same event as a separate module: the refused offsite transport for swallowed metal and the blanket request were not before the court as deliberate indifference claims, but they are the claims a better pleaded complaint would carry. Teach the posture: a nonprecedential order, decided on the prisoner's own allegations at screening, with the officers never served.

sections.note: No published California force decision for November 23 through 25. The one custody case on the week's published list, In re Kendall, is a habeas challenge to a prison disciplinary finding for possession of a controlled substance at High Desert State Prison, not a force case.

applications.title: A no contest plea does not end the civil case
applications.body: In the Ninth Circuit, after King v. Villegas, a prisoner or arrestee who pleads no contest to resisting under section 69 or section 148 may still sue for excessive force over the same incident, because the plea admits no facts. Agencies should stop treating that disposition as the end of the civil exposure and should assume the officers' reports will be tested against the complaint.

applications.title: Write the sequence, not the summary
applications.body: The court's analysis works moment by moment: what resistance preceded each application of force, and when the resistance stopped. The officers' reports in King described strikes, a push to the wall, a takedown, continued struggling, a radio call, leg control, compliance, and cuffs, in order. A report built that way is the one that survives a Heck motion or a trial.

applications.title: Put the photographs and the medical record in the file
applications.body: Photographs of the inmate and of staff were taken in King and none were in the record on appeal, while the complaint alleged a sergeant told medical staff to document a refusal of treatment. Injury photographs, both medical evaluations, and any refusal recorded in the inmate's own words are what answer that allegation.

applications.title: Do not block the camera; set a perimeter and apply it to everyone
applications.body: Recording a traffic stop from a gas pump is protected activity. In Berg a six second spotlight the bystander stepped out of was too trivial to support a claim, but other courts have found a blinding flashlight or an officer moving to block the lens sufficient. A perimeter is a reasonable restriction when it applies to everyone; the unaddressed allegation in Berg was that others were allowed closer.

applications.title: The words are the record
applications.body: "You must have no f*ckin' life, right?" got an officer reprimanded and quoted in a federal opinion. "We will see how you act tonight" is the line a prisoner in crisis heard as retaliation before he climbed onto his sink. "Wow that's a lot of spray" went into a complaint. Say what you would want read aloud in court, because it will be.

applications.title: Self-harm response: condition the force, use it on the behavior, stop when it stops
applications.body: The pepper spray in McNamara was approved because the instruction was conditional, the spray was used only when the prisoner resumed harming himself, and the force ended with handcuffs minutes later. State the condition out loud, document the behavior that met it, and get medical staff to the person. The opinion says nothing about quantity or decontamination; a record that does will be judged on them.

titles: He pleaded no contest to resisting. The Ninth Circuit says he can still sue for excessive force.
King v. Villegas: the en banc Ninth Circuit, a no contest plea, and "So long, Heck"
A no contest plea admits nothing. Why a prison force suit goes forward in the Ninth Circuit.

thumbnail.visual: the opinion line "a plaintiff who pleaded nolo to a state criminal charge will be bound to a factual narrative that was never proven and whose truth he never admitted. As we explain below, the answer is no." highlighted on a darkened page

videos.hook: On November 24, 2026, the full Ninth Circuit held that a Kern Valley State Prison inmate who pleaded no contest to resisting an officer may still sue two correctional officers for excessive force, because a no contest plea admits no facts and winning the force claim would not necessarily mean the conviction was invalid. The court overruled part of Sanders v. City of Pittsburg. Six judges joined the opinion, three concurred in the judgment and warned the ruling could keep Heck v. Humphrey from applying in no contest cases, and two dissented, one closing with "So long, Heck." For custody and patrol, the case is about what a resisting conviction no longer settles and what the report has to do instead.
videos.question: Does a no contest plea to resisting an officer end the prisoner's excessive force lawsuit?

quiz.q: In King v. Villegas, why did the en banc Ninth Circuit hold that Heck v. Humphrey did not bar the prisoner's excessive force suit after his no contest plea to resisting an officer?
options: Because Federal Rule of Evidence 410 made the plea inadmissible in the civil case

Because a no contest plea admits no facts, so there was no factual narrative binding him, and his allegations left room for a prima facie basis for the resisting charge at another point in the encounter
Because the officers' incident reports were not part of the state court record
Because the criminal charges were filed more than a year after the incident
quiz.teach: The court did not reach Rule 410. It held that a no contest plea is not an admission of factual guilt, that King was therefore bound to no narrative, and that his allegation of being struck while not resisting did not rule out resistance at another moment. Sanders v. City of Pittsburg was overruled to the extent it held otherwise.

quiz.q: What did Judge VanDyke's dissent in King v. Villegas call the approach of dividing one continuous officer and inmate encounter into separate moments for Heck purposes?
options: The continuous course of conduct rule
quiz.teach: Judge VanDyke wrote that "we've developed what I'll call the 'slice-and-dice' approach" and that the majority extended it to facts that only could exist. The majority's answer is that resistance "may precede or follow the excessive use of force by that same officer even within 'a single continuous chain of events lasting a very brief time.'" Both sides agree the conduct must be documented moment by moment.

quiz.q: In Berg v. Rivas, why did the Fifth Circuit hold that the officer's six second spotlight on the bystander's phone camera did not support a First Amendment retaliation claim?
options: Because recording the police is not protected activity in the Fifth Circuit
Because the bystander was inside the perimeter of the traffic stop
Because the interference was trivial: the officer turned the light on, the bystander stepped aside almost immediately, and he kept recording uninterrupted
Because the officer had been reprimanded by his department
quiz.teach: The court said the recording was protected and the case failed on the injury element. It distinguished a deputy who moved side to side to block a camera and a flashlight that saturated a camera's sensors, both of which were enough in other decisions. The rule for the street is to keep lights and bodies off the camera and to apply a perimeter to everyone.
